# Introduction to Zechariah

## Part 1: General Introduction

1. The eight night visions ([1:7–6:8](../01/07.md))

    * Four horns and four craftsmen ([1:18–21](../01/18.md))
    * The measuring line ([2:1–13](../02/01.md))
    * The priest in filthy clothes ([3:1–10](../03/01.md))
    * The golden lampstand olive trees ([4:1–14](../04/01.md))
    * The flying scroll ([5:1–4](../05/01.md))
    * The woman in a basket ([5:5–11](../05/05.md))
    * Four chariots ([6:1–8](../06/01.md))

1. Questions about fasting ([7:1–8:23](../07/01.md))

    * Yahweh comes as king ([14:1–21](../14/01.md))

### What is the Book of Zechariah about?

Zechariah wrote to the people of Judah who returned from being exiled in Babylon. The people of Judah continued to sin, as their ancestors did before they went into exile. Zechariah called the people to repent and to obey Yahweh. And he called them to renew the covenant with Yahweh. Zechariah also prophesied about the Messiah and about Israel finally being victorious over her enemies. (See: [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/covenant]])

### How should the title of this book be translated?

This book traditionally has been titled “Zechariah” or “The Book of Zechariah.” Translators may decide to call it the “The Book About Zechariah” or “The Sayings of Zechariah.” (See: [[rc://*/ta/man/translate/translate-names]])

### Who wrote the Book of Zechariah?

The prophet Zechariah wrote this book between 520 and 518 B.C.

## Part 2: Important Religious and Cultural Concepts

### Did Zechariah prophesy before Ezra, Nehemiah, and Haggai?

Zechariah prophesied before the time of Ezra and Nehemiah. He prophesied at the same time as Haggai and continued after Haggai.

## Part 3: Important Translation Issues

### What is the meaning of the term “Israel”?

The name “Israel” is used in many different ways in the Bible. Jacob was a son of Isaac. God changed Jacob’s name to Israel. The descendants of Jacob became a nation also called Israel. Eventually, the nation of Israel split into two kingdoms. The northern kingdom was named Israel. The southern kingdom was named Judah. Zechariah uses the term “Israel” to refer to both the nation of Israel and the northern kingdom of Israel.

### What imagery does Zechariah use in reference to the Messiah?

Zechariah presented the Messiah as both a king and a shepherd. Zechariah said that the Messiah would come and deliver his people. However, the Messiah would also be pierced ([12:10](../12/10.md)) and struck with the sword ([13:7](../13/07.md)). (See: [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/christ]])

### What does the phrase “that day” mean?

Zechariah often spoke of the last days by using the phrase “that day” or “in that day.” When referring to a future “day,” the translator should be aware that the author may be speaking about the last days. (See: [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/lastday]])

# Zechariah 1 General Notes

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter is written in prose mainly with imagery used throughout to portray Zechariah’s vision given by the Lord.

Some translations prefer to set apart quotations. The ULT and many other English translations set lines 1:3–6, 14–17, which are extended quotations, farther to the right on the page than the rest of the text.

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Visions

This book contains a number of visions given to Zechariah, so the images are not ones Zechariah actually saw but were given to him in a vision or dream. It is important for each of these visions to keep their meanings and not be interpreted to mean any specific thing.

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### Date

Zechariah uses two separate dates in this first chapter. When compared to the book of Haggai, Zechariah’s prophecy was proclaimed just a few weeks after Haggai. However, they prophesied in two different places: Haggai was in Jerusalem and Zechariah was somewhere outside of Jerusalem. (See: [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/prophet]])

# Zechariah 2 General Notes

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter is introduced in prose with imagery used in the rest of the chapter to portray Zechariah’s third vision about measuring lines given by the Lord.

Some translations prefer to set apart quotations. The ULT and many other English translations set the lines of 2:4–13, which are extended quotations, farther to the right on the page than the rest of the text.

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Visions

This book contains a number of visions given to Zechariah so the images are not ones Zechariah actually saw but were given to him in a vision or dream. It is important for each of these visions to keep their meanings and not be interpreted to mean any specific thing. Please be careful to translate each of the terms in your language.

The expression **I lifted up my eyes** was a common expression meaning “I looked up” or “I looked intently.” If this expression does not communicate well in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I looked up]

The word **behold** here alerts the reader to pay attention to the surprising information that follows. Your language may have a comparable expression that you could use here. Alternate translation: [and there was a man]

# Zechariah 4 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

Zechariah 4 is the fifth of eight night visions. The chapter moves from a prophetic vision (a golden lampstand with seven lamps and two olive trees) to an explanation, then to an oracle declaring that Zerubbabel will complete the temple “not by might and not by power, but by my Spirit,” and concludes with the identification of the two olive trees as those set apart to serve the Lord of all the earth.

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Temple Furniture as Symbol

The lampstand echoes the tabernacle menorah (Exodus 25:31–40). Seven lamps and continuous olive oil flowing through golden pipes symbolized God’s provision for continuous worship and the Spirit’s empowering presence.

### Anointing and Divine Empowering

“Sons of the fresh oil” is an idiom for those set apart for special service. Olive oil consecrated kings and priests; here it represents the Spirit enabling Zerubbabel and his community to complete the rebuilding work.

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### Quotations

Verses 6–10 contain a series of quotes where it is difficult to discern who is speaking. The ULT suggests:
- the angel speaks from 6–10
- the angel quotes Yahweh in the middle of verse 6 and beginning of verse 9
- the angel prophetically quotes the people’s reaction at the end of verse 7
- the angel, not Zechariah, is the speaker who received the word of Yahweh in verse 8
- the “me” at the end of verse 9 refers to the angel, this is probably the most contested point, scholars are divided as to if this is Zechariah, the angel speaking to him, or the Angel of Yahweh (read as Jesus)
If there is a translation in your area, you may wish to follow it’s decisions regarding speakers in this section. If not, you may wish to follow the ULT.

### Mountains as Obstacles

Verse 7 calls a “great mountain” to become “a plain,” representing political and practical obstacles dissolving so that Zerubbabel can set the capstone in place.

# Zechariah 5 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter presents two [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/other/vision]]s in which an [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/angel]] interprets what Zechariah sees. The first vision (verses 1–4) shows a flying [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/other/scroll]] carrying a divine [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/curse]] against thieves and false swearers. The second vision (verses 5–11) shows [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/evil]] personified as a woman sealed inside an ephah and carried away to [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/names/shinar]].

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Personification of Wickedness

# Zechariah 6 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter concludes the eight night visions (vv. 1-8) with four [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/other/chariot]]s dispatched as divine agents, then shifts to a sign-act in which Zechariah [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/other/crown]]s Joshua the high [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/priest]] and delivers the “Branch” oracle (vv. 9-15).

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### The Branch

The title “Branch” (צֶּמַח) is a messianic designation for a coming king who will build the [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/temple]] and unite kingship and priesthood on one [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/other/throne]], with “a counsel of [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/other/peace]]” between the two offices (vv. 12-13).

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### Nested Quotations

Verses 10-15 contain three levels of quotation as Yahweh instructs Zechariah to speak to Joshua a message from Yahweh of Armies.

# Zechariah 6 General Notes

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter is written mainly in prose and tells the last vision of the four chariots in the first part of the chapter.

Some translations set each line of poetry farther to the right than the rest of the text to make it easier to read. The ULT does this with the poetic song in 6:12–13.

# Zechariah 7 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

Zechariah 7 shifts from prophetic visions to prose narrative. A delegation from Bethel asks whether to continue [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/other/fast|fasting]] in the fifth month, and Yahweh responds with two oracles (vv. 4-7, 8-14) that redirect the question from ritual observance to [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/justice|justice]], [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/covenantfaith|covenant faithfulness]], and [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/mercy|mercy]].

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Fasting as Ritual Mourning

The fifth-month fast commemorated the destruction of Solomon’s temple. Yahweh challenges whether this practice honored him or merely served the people themselves.

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### Nested Quotation Levels

Verses 5-7 and 9-10 contain three levels of quotation (narrator, Yahweh, inner message), requiring careful management of quotation marking conventions.

You could convert the Hebrew day and month into an approximate date on the calendar that your culture uses. # Zechariah 8 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter presents a series of prophetic oracles introduced by the messenger formula “Thus says Yahweh of Armies,” moving from Yahweh’s commitment to Zion (vv. 1-8) through encouragement to rebuild the [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/temple]] (vv. 9-15), ethical demands (vv. 16-17), and a vision of the nations seeking Yahweh (vv. 18-23).

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Fasts Becoming Festivals

The four [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/other/fast]] days commemorating Jerusalem’s fall will become joyful celebrations when Yahweh restores his people.

# Zechariah 9 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter is a prophetic oracle (the “burden of the word of Yahweh”) that moves from judgment on the surrounding nations (verses 1-8), to the coming of a righteous, humble [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/other/king]] who brings peace (verses 9-10), to Yahweh’s deliverance and restoration of his people (verses 11-17).

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### The blood of the covenant

In verse 11, “the blood of your [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/covenant]]” refers to the sacrifices that ratified Yahweh’s agreement with Israel, the basis for his freeing his people.

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### Verse 1
The first verse has several difficulties. The first set center on Yahweh’s relationship with Hadrach and Damascus. Many English Bibles translate the preposition here (Yahweh *in* the land) as ‘against’ but that preposition does not usually mean that. It is also not clear what is resting in Damascus. Is it Yahweh or his word or the burden? What does it mean to be his resting place? For the first set, the text and notes will lean toward an interpretation like, “this prophecy is about some place near Hadrach and Damascus, Yahweh is especially present there right now because he is about to do something.” The second set of difficulties center on the question of whose eyes are looking at whom? Is Yahweh watching the world and Israelites closely? Are the world and the Israelites watching Yahweh closely (as verse 5 may suggest)? Why (beyond translation)? The text and notes will lean toward the interpretation that Yahweh is watching the world closely. This seems to hold with other parts of the book (4:10, 12:4)  and verse 8. If a local translation makes a clear decision, you may wish to follow that. Otherwise you may wish to follow the decisions made here.

### Shifting speakers and personified cities

The speaker shifts between the prophet and Yahweh (first person), and cities such as Tyre and Ekron are personified as women; track these shifts throughout the chapter.

### The Lord
In verse 4 and 14 Yahweh is referred to as “Lord.” While we do not recommend following the custom of translating Yahweh as Lᴏʀᴅ, if that is the decision your translation has made, you will need to take special care in verse 14 where the text reads “the Lord Yahweh” and follow how you have translated that combination in other places (Ezekiel).

# Zechariah 10 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This prophetic poem first contrasts Yahweh, who gives rain and guidance, with worthless idols and diviners (verses 1-2), then becomes a first-person divine promise to strengthen and regather his scattered people (verses 3-12).

# Zechariah 13 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

Verses 1–6 are a prose oracle about cleansing from sin and removing false [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/prophet|prophets]]. Verses 7–9 shift to poetry, announcing the striking of Yahweh’s [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/other/shepherd|shepherd]] and the [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/purify|purifying]] of a surviving [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/remnant|remnant]].

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### The Prophetic Cloak

The “cloak of hair” (verse 4) is the rough garment that identified [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/prophet|prophets]]. False prophets abandon this clothing to conceal their identity.

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

Zechariah often speaks of the last days by using the phrase “that day” or “in that day.” When referencing a future “day,” the translator should be aware that it is possible that the author is speaking about the last days.
